title: High-speed Si-Ge avalanche photodiode with a gain-bandwidth product of 7564 GHz

paper_content.introduction:
Avalanche photodetectors are highly valued for their high bandwidth, high gain, and compact integration, making them
widely applicable in optical communications, optical interconnects, light detection and ranging (LiDAR) systems,
quantum computing, and biosensing1-3. As artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and cloud computing continue
to expand rapidly, the demand for computational power and high-speed data transmission in large-scale data centers and
high-performance computing (HPC) is growing exponentially4-6. This surge has intensified the need for transceivers with
higher bandwidth density. However, current optical link and power budgets are struggling to keep pace with these
escalating demands4. As a pivotal component in optical receivers, APDs play a crucial role in enhancing link performance
by providing internal gain, which helps reduce power consumption and optimize signal integrity. These characteristics
are essential for advancing optical receiver systems toward higher bandwidth and lower power operation7,8.

Gain bandwidth product (GBP) is a key metric in evaluating APD performance in high-speed optical communication
and is strongly influenced by the impact ionization coefficient ratio. While most III-V materials exhibit an impact
ionization coefficient ratio in the range of k ≈ 0.1-19,10 , silicon (Si) stands out with an exceptionally low ratio of k ≈
0.0211,12. However, Si’s cutoff wavelength of 1100 nm limits efficient photo-carrier generation in fiber communication
wavelengths, necessitating alternative materials. Germanium (Ge) is a preferred material for silicon-based PDs due to its
superior absorption efficiency at fiber communication wavelengths and higher carrier mobility compared to Si. However,
the impact ionization coefficient ratio of Ge (k ≈ 1)13,14 is significantly higher, potentially leading to increased noise. To
leverage the high absorption of Ge while benefiting from the low ionization coefficient ratio of Si, researchers have
proposed APDs with separate absorption charge multiplication (SACM) structures15. Fabricated on a standard silicon-
on-insulator (SOI) platform, the Si-Ge APD offers higher gain, excellent sensitivity, and superior integration density,
making it an optimal choice for high-performance optical receivers16,17.

In current SACM structure research, vertical SACM-type APDs require metal electrode deposition on the Ge
surface18,19. However, this approach induces Fermi-level pinning, degrading the ohmic contact and increasing contact
resistance. Additionally, the metal presence on the Ge surface introduces more dangling bonds, leading to higher leakage
current, which in turn reduces device responsivity and increases noise. Moreover, metal contacts facilitate additional
photogenerated carrier recombination, further compromising optoelectronic performance. In contrast, lateral SACM Si-
Ge APDs mitigate these challenges while also simplifying fabrication. Dai et al. proposed a series of lateral SACM Si-
Ge APDs, demonstrating a significant GBP improvement from 615 GHz20 to 1440 GHz21, and later to 3036 GHz22. This
progression has provided valuable insights into GBP enhancement strategies. However, this design still exhibits relatively
high dark current at the operating voltage, which can hinder the achievement of higher sensitivity and gain. A recent
study reported an improved lateral SACM Si-Ge APD with a bandwidth of 53 GHz and a GBP of 1033 GHz23. The high
bandwidth was achieved by incorporating a large inductor (~700 pH) into the APD electrode through inductive peaking.
However, in the SACM structure, the multiplication gain and GBP remain constrained by the Ge-Si doping contact due
to the high dark current resulting from significant tunneling currents at high voltages. Additionally, this approach may
introduce challenges in impedance matching with the transimpedance amplifier S(TIA) and signal transmission. Currently,
researchers continue exploring various strategies to further enhance APSD GBP for higher-speed and higher-gain
detection24. However, achieving a significantly higher GBP remains a crEitical and challenging research direction.

In this work, we present a high-speed Si-Ge APD with a reRcord-breaking GBP of 7564 GHz, which exceeds
previously reported values. Utilizing a lateral SACM structurPe, we design an APD that spatially separates the Ge
absorption region from the doped regions. By minimizing th e electric field in Ge while maintaining efficient carrier
transport and multiplication, the dark current is significantly reduced. To further enhance device responsivity, we
incorporate a tapered waveguide at the front end and a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) at the rear. Experimental results
show that under a reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V, Ethe APD exhibits a dark current of 8.4 μA and achieves a maximum
GBP of 7564 GHz at an input optical power of L-24 dBm, while maintaining a low effective k value of 0.05. We evaluate
the APD performance for high-speed signals and obtain clear eye diagrams for 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps non-return-to-
zero (NRZ) signals, as well as 128 Gbps and 200 Gbps four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) signals. The APD
also exhibits high sensitivity, achieving -20.8 dBm and -17.1 dBm for 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps NRZ signals, respectively,
both of which meet the hard-decision forward error correction (HD-FEC) threshold of BER = 3.8×10−3. For 128 Gbps
and 200 Gbps PAM4 signals, the sensitivities are -14.2 dBm and -9.6 dBm, respectively, both within the HD-FEC limit.
Furthermore, we perform high-speed eye diagram measurements for 200 Gbps PAM4 signals across eight APDs, each
tuned to the specific wavelengths required for eight-channel dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM). This
manuscript represents a substantial extension of our previous OFC work25, expanding the study from a single-channel
device to an eight-channel APD array, and providing detailed design and analysis, along with a further systematic
investigation of excess-noise characteristics. These remarkable results highlight the immense potential of this APD for
applications in optical communications, quantum technology, LiDAR, and beyond.
paper_content.results:
Device Structure and Design
Figure 1(a) presents a three-dimensional (3D) schematic of the lateral p+-i-p-n+ doped SACM Si-Ge APD, incorporating
a DBR at the rear to enhance device responsivity. The design process begins with optimizing the electric field distribution
to achieve high performance. Figure 1(b) illustrates the cross-sectional doping profile of the Si-Ge APD, featuring a non-
contact design between the Ge region and the Si-doped areas to effectively control the electric field within the Ge. To
quantitatively describe this non-contact design strategy, we optimize the doping positions on the rib waveguide, denoted
as Wp and ΔW, respectively. Additionally, thicker metal interconnects are employed to further enhance device
performance. The Ge absorption region dimensions are 9.1 μm (length) × 0.5 μm (width) × 0.26 μm (height). Given Ge's
high impact ionization coefficient, optimization efforts focus on the doping regions adjacent to the Ge layer, specifically
adjusting the widths of Wp and ΔW. The primary goal is to maximize ionization within Si while suppressing ionization
in Ge, requiring the electric field strength in Si to exceed 3×10⁷ V/m, while ensuring it remains below 2×10⁷ V/m in
Ge26,27. Additionally, to facilitate efficient carrier transport at saturation velocity within Ge, the electric field in Ge is
designed to exceed 1×10⁶ V/m 28.

The electric field design begins with optimizing the multiplication region doping width Wp to maintain a high
electric field within the multiplication region while preventing its extension into the absorption region. Figure 1(c) depicts
the electric field distribution along the black cutline of the ridge waveguide in Figure 1(b) under varying Wp conditions.
As the Wp increases, the electric field strength in the multiplication region rises, but the high electric field region
gradually shifts toward the absorption region, potentially increasing the electric field in Ge and degrading device
performance. To balance these effects, Wp is set at 225 nm. Next, ΔW is optimized to confine the electric field effectively
within the charge region. Figure 1(d) illustrates the electric field distribution along the black cutline of the ridge
waveguide in Figure 1(b) under different p+ doping width conditions, with anS inset providing a magnified view of the
localized region. If the doping position is too far from the Ge layer, the eSlectric field is not fully confined within the
charge region, potentially inducing additional current in the Si-doped arEea and increasing the device's shot noise. Based
on the above considerations, i.e., to ensure effective confinement ofR the optical field, ΔW is set to 110 nm.

To further enhance performance, graded doping is emploPyed to reduce resistance and capacitance. The p-type
doping concentrations are set at 7.1 × 1019 cm-3 (p++), 5.3 × 1018 cm-3 (p+), and 2.1 × 1017 cm-3 (p), while the n-type
doping concentrations are set at 1.0 × 1020 cm-3 (n++) and 1.0 × 1019 cm-3 (n+), respectively. Additionally, a lateral
structure is adopted to minimize light absorption by metal electrodes and reduce dark current caused by defects near the
heterojunction under breakdown voltage conditioEns. The inset in Figure 1(b) presents the simulated cross-sectional
electric field results under a reverse bias of 12.L5 V, confirming effective electric field confinement. Through optimized
doping position and concentration, together with precise control of Wp and ΔW enabled by the non-contact design, the
high electric field is effectively confined within the Si multiplication region, while the Ge absorption region is maintained
at a relatively low electric field, thereby achieving precise electric-field engineering. Under this field configuration,
avalanche multiplication is dominated by an electron-driven quasi-unipolar mechanism, in which impact ionization in Si
is maximized whereas ionization in Ge is strongly suppressed. As a result, the excess noise is effectively reduced and the
overall device performance is significantly enhanced.

The APD couples O-band optical signals from the Si waveguide into Ge. To mitigate coupling loss caused by abrupt
width changes between the Si and Ge waveguides, a tapered waveguide is employed. Traditionally, increasing Ge volume
has been a primary method for enhancing responsivity. However, as the volume of Ge increases, the carrier transit time
is prolonged, reducing the response speed and adversely impacting the device's electrical performance. To address this
issue, we integrate a DBR at the rear and incorporated a tapered waveguide at the front to confine more light within the
absorption region, thereby enabling secondary light absorption and improving overall responsivity.

The DBR structure in this device is a first-order DBR, chosen for its low scattering losses and high reflectivity. As
depicted in Figure 1(e), when the number of grating periods reaches five, the reflectivity exceeds 90%, effectively
reflecting light at the tail. The inset in Figure 1(e) illustrates that, with five grating periods, the operational wavelength
range extends from 1100 nm to 1700 nm, perfectly covering the O-band. Figure 2 presents 3D finite-difference time-
domain (FDTD) simulation results for two APD structures. The evanescently coupled optical field distributions for APDs
without and with a DBR are shown in Figures 2(a) and (c), respectively. In the absence of a DBR, significant light leakage
occurs at the end of the APD. In contrast, incorporating a DBR significantly reduces this leakage by reflecting the
unabsorbed light back into the Ge region, thereby enhancing responsivity. To fully utilize this reflective effect, the Ge
length is optimized to 9.1 μm (see Supplementary Note 1), rather than 9.0 μm or 9.2 μm, as this specific length allows
more unabsorbed light to be reflected and reabsorbed during a second pass. However, standing waves are observed in
the field distribution, mainly due to mode mismatch between the Si waveguide and Ge layer as well as reflections from
the rear DBR. Simulations indicate that the optical return loss (ORL) of this device is -22.5 dB (see Supplementary Note
2). To further verify the effect of the DBR, top-view field distributions in Figures 2(b) and 2(d) show that the inclusion
of the DBR significantly increases the optical intensity in the Ge absorption region. The inclusion of a five-period DBR
at the rear enhances the overall light confinement within the Ge layer. Additionally, a front-end tapered waveguide is
employed to minimize input reflection losses. As a result, the device's responsivity improves by 35%.

Static Measurements

incident light, with optical power ranging from -26 dBm to -12 dBm. The grating couplers (GCs) used in this work are
characterized using a test structure consisting of a pair of GCs connected by a short straight waveguide. The measured
insertion loss is 6.0 dB/facet at 1310 nm. At a reverse bias of 3.5 V, the APD exShibits an optical internal responsivity of
0.75 A/W at unit gain, determined by comparison with a reference p-i-n PSD fabricated on the same chip and sharing
identical structural parameters (see Supplementary Note 3), includingE Ge volume, waveguide dimensions, and GC

to accommodate the bandwidth limitations imposed by a largeP Ge volume, part of the responsivity is intentionally
sacrificed. The dark current initially increases gradually and th en rises sharply as the voltage approaches breakdown. At
a reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V, the dark current remains low at 8.4 μA, allowing the device to achieve exceptionally
high multiplication gain. The breakdown voltage of the Si-Ge APD is 13 V, corresponding to a dark current of 100 μA20.

Small-Signal Measurements
To characterize the optoelectronic (OE) bandwidth of the APD through small-signal measurements, the test setup is
illustrated in Figure 4(a). The optical signal emitted by the O-band laser is first directed into a lightwave component
analyzer (LCA), then sequentially passes through a handheld variable optical attenuator (VOA) and a polarization
controller (PC), before being vertically coupled into the device under test (DUT) via a GC. Figures 4(c) and 4(d) show
the physical photograph and a cross-sectional scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of the APD, respectively. The
photocurrent generated by the APD is routed back to the LCA through a bias-tee to measure the bandwidth. As shown in
Figure 3(c), when the input optical power is -24 dBm, the APD exhibits a 3-dB OE bandwidth of 8 GHz at a reverse bias
of 7 V, primarily due to incomplete depletion of the Ge absorption region. As the reverse bias voltage increases, the 3 dB
OE bandwidth gradually increases, reaching a maximum of 31 GHz at a reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V. However, with
further increases in reverse bias, the 3 dB OE bandwidth starts to decrease, primarily due to the dominance of the
avalanche buildup time in the frequency response of the APD. The inset of Figure 3(c) shows the variation of the 3-dB
OE bandwidth under input optical powers ranging from -26 dBm to -12 dBm at a fixed reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V.
As the input optical power decreases, the bandwidth gradually reduces. At -26 dBm, the bandwidth is 30 GHz,
representing a 16.6% reduction compared to -12 dBm. This behavior arises because, at lower input optical powers, the
generation and collection of photogenerated carriers slow down, limiting the APD response speed and consequently
reducing the 3-dB bandwidth. Figure 3(d) illustrates the multiplication gain and GBP characteristics at reverse bias
voltages of 9 V, 10 V, 11 V, 12 V, and 12.5 V, corresponding to five different multiplication gain points for input optical
power levels ranging from -12 dBm to -24 dBm. At an input power of -16 dBm and a reverse bias of 12.5 V, the APD
achieves a multiplication gain of 73 and a 3 dB OE bandwidth of 36 GHz, corresponding to a maximum GBP of 2628
GHz. When the input power is reduced to -24 dBm at the same 12.5 V reverse bias, the GBP of the APD increases to
7564 GHz. The inset of Figure 3(d) shows the trends of gain and bandwidth at an input optical power of -24 dBm. Both
metrics increase with bias voltage until peaking, after which they decline. This degradation is attibuted to excessive noise
and prolonged avalanche build-up time at high voltages, which deteriorate the APD’s performance.

GBP of APDs increases2,5,13,40. This clear trend indicates that a lower k value effectively suppresses excess noise under
high multiplication gain, which is critical for achieving higher GBP in APDs41.

Eye Diagram and Bit Error Rate Measurements
To assess the signal reception quality, an eye diagram measurement was conducted. Figure 4(b) shows the
experimental setup for measuring the APD eye diagram and bit error rate (BER). An O-band tunable laser was used as
the optical source. The optical signal first passed through a PC and was then modulated by a thin-film lithium niobate
(TFLN) Mach-Zehnder modulator (MZM), which was driven by an amplified high-speed electrical signal. After a second
PC for polarization adjustment, the modulated optical signal was vertically coupled into the DUT via a GC. The
photocurrent generated by the APD was directed through a bias-tee to an oscilloscope for eye diagram and TDECQ
analysis, and then sent to a BER tester to assess the APD’s sensitivity.

The eye diagram measurements were conducted with an input optical power of -16 dBm and a reverse bias voltage
of 12.5 V, with no TIA connected to the APD. Figures 5(a) and 5(b) present the eye diagrams measured at data rates of
64 Gbps NRZ and 100 Gbps NRZ, with signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) of 8.26 dB and 6.08 dB, respectively. Figures 5(c)
and 5(d) show the eye diagrams for data rates of 128 Gbps PAM4 and 200 Gbps PAM4, with PAM4 transmitter and
dispersion eye closure quaternary (TDECQ) values of 1.88 dB and 3.23 dB, respectively.

To evaluate the sensitivity of the APD, BER tests were conducted. The upper partion of Figure 5(e) shows the BER
performance for NRZ signals at 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps with a reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V. The corresponding
sensitivities at the HD-FEC threshold were measured as -20.8 dBm and -17.1 dBm, respectively. The lower partion of
Figure 5(e) illustrates the sensitivities for PAM4 signals at 100 Gbps and 200 Gbps under the same bias voltage, with
sensitivies of -14.2 dBm and -9.6 dBm, respectively, at the HD-FEC threshold. These results highlight the APD’s strong
competitiveness for high-bandwidth and energy-efficient data transmission applications.

Wavelength Division Multiplexing Measurements
Finally, to demonstrate the WDM capability and channel uniformity of the proposed device, we employed an eight-
channel APD array (Figure 6(a)) in combination with an external DWDM demultiplexer with a channel spacing of 200
GHz (≈1.14 nm in the O-band). In the present proof-of-concept experiment, the demultiplexed channels were
characterized sequentially. The demultiplexed wavelengths of λ₁ = 1305.92 nm, λ₂ = 1307.06 nm, λ₃ = 1308.20 nm, λ₄ =
1309.34 nm, λ₅ = 1310.48 nm, λ₆ = 1311.62 nm, λ₇ = 1312.76 nm, and λ₈ = 1313.90 nm were successfully detected.
Owing to the narrow wavelength span (<10 nm) of the eight DWDM chanSnels, the measured responsivity shows
negligible wavelength dependence. Clear eye diagrams were obtained for aSll eight channels at a data rate of 200 Gbps
PAM4, as shown in Figure 6(b), demonstrating the broadband capabilityE and good uniformity of the APD array.
paper_content.methods:
Device Fabrication
The APD was fabricated on a 130-nm SOI platform, and a schematic cross-section of the device is shown in Fig. 1b. The
Si waveguide was formed by etching the 220-nm-thick top Si layer, with an etch depth of 70 nm as shown in the figure.
After waveguide etching, ion implantation was peErformed to dope the Si waveguide. Subsequently, a 260-nm-thick Ge
absorption layer was epitaxially grown on the Ldoped Si waveguide. Tungsten was then used to form ohmic contacts to
the heavily doped regions, followed by copper metallization for vias and interconnects. Finally, an Al layer was deposited
to form the contact pads.

Eye Diagram Measurements
The experimental setup for the eye-diagram measurement is shown in Fig. 4b. During the measurements, the frequency
response of the test link was calibrated and compensated using a Keysight M8194A arbitrary waveform generator (AWG),
resulting in a relatively flat frequency response of the entire electrical-optical-electrical link within a 40 GHz bandwidth
and effectively minimizing the influence of external link components. A PRBS-11 data pattern (211-1 bits) generated by
the AWG was used for all eye-diagram measurements.

The measurement setup employed a full high-speed Radio Frequency (RF) chain, including RF probes, RF cables,
bias-tees, TFLN MZMs, and RF amplifiers, all with bandwidths exceeding 67 GHz. No TIA was integrated after the
APD, and no external digital signal processing (DSP) or offline equalization was applied. Only the built-in real-time
forward equalization (5 taps) and filtering functions of the sampling oscilloscope were enabled during the measurements.
These signal-processing functions effectively compensate for frequency roll-off and mitigate inter-symbol interference,
thereby providing effective system bandwidth for the successful reception of 200 Gbps PAM-4 signals and enabling clear
eye openings, despite the intrinsic small-signal 3-dB bandwidth of the APD being below 40 GHz.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: This is an interesting paper. The authors report a Ge-Si avalanche photodiode (APD) having a separate absorption, charge, and multiplication (SACM) structure. This lateral structure is similar to those reported in references 21-23. A novel feature of the present work is that the authors use a graded waveguide at the device input and a Bragg grating at the output to improve responsivity. The authors claim a record gain-bandwidth product > 8700. The receiver measurements are impressive. However, two major issues should be addressed before I can recommend publication. 1. Measurements of the gain bandwidth product require accurately determining the unity gain point. That the authors have accomplished this is doubtful. They state that the unity gain point occurs at a bias of 3.5 V. First, there is no indication of how this is determined. It certainly is not obvious from the photocurrent curves. While the photocurrent curves continue to increase with higher bias from that point, there is no proof that the authors are not observing a combination of increased responsivity from increasing the field in the Ge absorber and increasing impact ionization. It is frequently observed, however, that in APDs the low-bias portion of the photocurrent increases linearly with voltage due to the penetration of the depletion region into the photo-generation region [M. H. Woods, et al., IEEE Solid-State Electron., vol. 16, pp. 381–394.] This reduces the distance that photo-generated minority carriers travel before entering the depletion region and thus increases the injected minority carrier diffusion current. For example, it was found that the low-bias electron injection photocurrent curves in InP APDs consisted of an exponential voltage-dependent portion followed by a linear region [L. W. Cook, et al., Gallium Arsenide Related Compounds, pp. 281–286, 1981 and G. E. Bulman, et al., Solid-State Electron., vol. 25, no. 12, pp. 1189–1200, 1982]. When describing their bandwidth measurements, the authors in the present work note that the absorber is not fully depleted at 7 V bias. The most straightforward method to determine the gain at low bias is to measure the noise and carry out a two-parameter fit to k and gain. At present, the authors’ designations of gain and gain-bandwidth product are not credible. 2. The authors note that using the back grating and tapered input increases the responsivity by 35%. They also quote a unity gain responsivity of 0.75 A/W. It is difficult to believe that this is the external responsivity. What is the estimated input coupling efficiency? If these APDs are to be implemented in practical systems, knowing how much light is lost to input coupling is important. As an extreme example, a detector with an internal quantum efficiency of 100% and an input coupling efficiency of – 10 dB is not very useful.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: This paper presents a lateral separate absorption charge multiplication (SACM) silicon-germanium (SiGe) APD designed for operation in the O-band, demonstrating a dark current of ~8.4 μA at 12.5 V and a high GBP of 8784 GHz as well as high bit rate data receiving. Indeed, high GBP APD is really important and attractive for various applications. More efforts should be made to enhance the device performance when possible. There are some comments below to be addressed before it can be re-considered. 1. This paper utilizes the lateral separate absorption charge multiplication (SACM) structure (Fig. 1a and 1b). The reviewer noticed that the structure in Fig. 1b is exactly the same as that proposed in ref. 20-Optica 9, 762-769, 2022 (Fig. 1b, see below). The authors just made a left-right flip. When describing the device structure in the manuscript, the authors should cite ref. 20 and tell that they are exactly the same. Fig. 1b from this manuscript submitted to NC. Fig. 1b from ref. 20 (Optica 9, 762-769, 2022). 2. Actually, Ge has very high absorption coefficient in the O-band. Light can be absorbed completely almost when the length is 8-9μm, as demonstrated previously. Figure 1(f) shows the simulated light propagation in the structures with and without a reflector. However, the authors should give the results about the light absorption in the Ge/Si active region, and compare the difference between the designs with and without the reflector. 3. The authors should label the light propagation direction in Fig. 1(f) to be clarified. From Fig. 1(f), light is reflected back and there are notable interference patterns even in the passive input section, indicating that some light is reflected back to the input port. Such kind of reflection is detrimental for the optical link. This reflection should be double-checked. Basically speaking, it is expected to have very complete light absorption because of the light absorption is enhanced by the forward and backward propagation. 4. The authors claimed “The APD couples O-band optical signals from the Si waveguide into Ge, but conventional coupling efficiency is relatively low”. What is “conventional”? Please clarify it. As demonstrated in Fig. 1(a), there is no special structure for the connection between the passive silicon waveguide and the Ge/Si active region. 5. More details should be given for the experimental results. For example, what is the optical power for Fig. 2(c). The frequency response would become different when operating at different optical powers. Basically, when the optical power decreases, the 3-dB bandwidth might be reduced. Please show the measured 3-dB bandwidths for the cases with different powers. 6. The authors claimed “At a reverse bias of 3.5 V, the APD exhibits an optical responsivity of 0.75 A/W at unit gain, determined by comparing its responsivity to that of a reference p-i-n PD on the same chip”. Since the authors have added reflector at the rear to enhance the light absorption, please explain why the responsivity of the reference p-i-n PD is as low as 0.75 A/W, which is far less than those reported previously (e.g., 0.9~1.0A/W). 7. What is the efficiency for the fiber-chip coupling? It is one of the key for evaluating the responsivity of the PD/APD. Please check how accurately can the coupling efficiency be measured? 8. Could the author explain the strategy for reducing the dark current? Also please give an analysis about the noise. 9. The data about the GBP at the optical power of -12, -14 dBm should be given in Fig. 2(d). 10. About the bandwidths in Fig. 2(c). It can be seen that the bandwidths for the bias voltages of 9, 10, 11V are almost the same but as low as ~18 GHz. When the bias voltage increases to 12V, the 3-dB bandwidth increases rapidly to ~25 GHz. Please give an explanation about this. 11. Please show the result of the measured 3-dB bandwidth as the gain varies. 12. Please comment the polarization dependence of the present APD, which would be important for a receiver. 13. The authors claimed “At an input power of -16 dBm and a reverse bias of 12.5 V, the APD achieves a multiplication gain of 73 and a 3 dB OE bandwidth of 36 GHz, corresponding to a maximum GBP of 2628 GHz. Reply to Reviewers Comments
Manuscript ID: NCOMMS-25-17798
Title: A High-Speed Si-Ge Avalanche Photodiode with a Gain-Bandwidth Product
of 7564 GHz
On behalf of all the authors, I would like to extend our sincere thanks to the
reviewers for their constructive and insightful comments on our manuscript. These
suggestions have been highly valuable and have played an important role in improving
the overall quality of our work. In response to the reviewers’ feedback, we have
thoroughly revised the manuscript and incorporated additional data to strengthen the
validity of our results. Additionally, we have streamlined the abstract to better align
with the journal's requirements. We now submitting a revised version of the manuscript
that reflects all the reviewers’ recommendations.
As detailed below, we have provided a point-by-point response to each of the
reviewers’ comments and suggestions. For ease of communication, the reviewers’
comments are presented in bold black, while our responses are shown in blue. The
corresponding revisions in the manuscript are marked in red. References cited in the
response are formatted in black italics.
Once again, we sincerely appreciate your positive evaluation and the valuable
suggestions that have contributed to enhancing the quality of our manuscript.
Reviewer 1
1. Measurements of the gain bandwidth product require accurately determining
the unity gain point. That the authors have accomplished this is doubtful. They
state that the unity gain point occurs at a bias of 3.5 V. First, there is no indication
of how this is determined. It certainly is not obvious from the photocurrent curves.
While the photocurrent curves continue to increase with higher bias from that
point, there is no proof that the authors are not observing a combination of
increased responsivity from increasing the field in the Ge absorber and increasing
impact ionization. It is frequently observed, however, that in APDs the low-bias
portion of the photocurrent increases linearly with voltage due to the penetration
of the depletion region into the photo-generation region [M. H. Woods, et al., IEEE
Solid-State Electron., vol. 16, pp. 381–394.] This reduces the distance that photo-
generated minority carriers travel before entering the depletion region and thus
increases the injected minority carrier diffusion current. For example, it was
found that the low-bias electron injection photocurrent curves in InP APDs
consisted of an exponential voltage-dependent portion followed by a linear region
[L. W. Cook, et al., Gallium Arsenide Related Compounds, pp. 281–286, 1981 and
G. E. Bulman, et al., Solid-State Electron., vol. 25, no. 12, pp. 1189–1200, 1982].
When describing their bandwidth measurements, the authors in the present work
note that the absorber is not fully depleted at 7 V bias. The most straightforward
method to determine the gain at low bias is to measure the noise and carry out a
two-parameter fit to k and gain. At present, the authors’ designations of gain and
gain-bandwidth product are not credible.
Response:
We are deeply appreciative of your attention to our work and the valuable feedback
you have provided. The method you suggested for determining the unit multiplication
point by measuring noise is indeed viable. However, it necessitates the use of a noise
figure analyzer. Regrettably, our laboratory does not currently possess this instrument,
and thus, we are unable to conduct the relevant experiments.
As you have pointed out, under low bias conditions, the junction region may not
be fully depleted, and the quantum efficiency may not reach saturation. Therefore, the
increase in photocurrent I with bias voltage could be attributed to the combined
ph
increase in both quantum efficiency and gain G, making it challenging to distinguish
between these two mechanisms. Hence, accurately determining the unit gain point in
an APD is of paramount importance.
To our knowledge, in the current Si-Ge material system, in addition to the method
you mentioned for determining the unit multiplication point, there are two other
methods. The first method involves estimating the unit gain point by measuring the
point where the second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to bias becomes zero
[1, 2]. We measured the photocurrent at an input optical power of -12 dBm and
performed local amplification, with the results shown in Figure 1. From the figure, it
can be observed that the unit multiplication point is reached at a voltage of 3.5 V.
The second method is the one we employed in our initial draft: determining the
unit multiplication point by comparing the responsivity of a PIN PD fabricated on the
same die and sharing identical structural parameters (such as the length, width, and
thickness of the Ge absorption region, as well as the length and width of the Si
waveguide). Currently, this method has been widely accepted and recognized by many
prior works, including Nature Photonics [3, 4], Optica [5], Optical Fiber
Communication Conference (OFC) [6], and European Conference on Optical
Communication (ECOC) [7].
This method is considered reliable because the responsivity of the PD is primarily
determined by the length of the Ge region and the coupling area. Although doping can
influence responsivity to some extent, the two devices in our comparison share exactly
the same heavily doped regions (in terms of concentration, area, and spacing). The only
difference lies in the lightly doped region, where n-type doping is replaced by p-type
doping. However, the influence of light doping on responsivity is minimal. Under such
conditions, the responsivity measured from the PIN device is nearly identical to the
initial responsivity of the APD.
Therefore, we believe that this method provides a reliable means of characterizing
APD performance. Notably, the method adopted in our initial draft is consistent with
those used in previous studies, suggesting that applying consistent testing and
characterization methods for gain-bandwidth product comparisons is reasonable.
Furthermore, a comparison of results from both methods yielded the same unit gain
point of 3.5 V, which supports the validity of our characterization approach.
On the other hand, to address your questions regarding gain measurement, we have
supplemented more detailed experimental testing and calculation methods. In the
experiment, we used experimental equipment such as a source meter, a probe station, a
tunable laser, and a variable optical attenuator, with the experimental setup shown in
Figure 2. We measured the photocurrent Iph at 1310 nm for received optical powers
ranging from -26 to -12 dBm, and simultaneously measured the dark current Id in the
absence of optical input. Subsequently, we calculated the multiplication gain G(V)
according to the following formula, that is, the ratio of the net photocurrent (Iph−Id) at
bias V to the net photocurrent measured at the unit gain point of V :

method has also been used to calculate gain in numerous papers [6,8,9].

clarified. From Fig. 1(f), light is reflected back and there are notable interference
patterns even in the passive input section, indicating that some light is reflected
back to the input port. Such kind of reflection is detrimental for the optical link.
This reflection should be double-checked. Basically speaking, it is expected to have
very complete light absorption because of the light absorption is enhanced by the
forward and backward propagation.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate your careful review of our manuscript and the valuable
comments you provided. Regarding the issue you raised about the direction of light
propagation, we have made the necessary corrections in the revised manuscript. The
updated results are shown in Figures 4(a) and 4(c), where the Ge absorption region is
highlighted with a red dashed box, as also indicated in the revised text.
Regarding the interference issue you mentioned, it is primarily caused by reflected
waves and is, to some extent, unavoidable. In the case of this APD, there are two main
contributing factors:
1. Mode mismatch: The PD employs evanescent coupling from a Si waveguide
into the Ge absorption layer. Due to the difference in effective refractive indices
between the Si waveguide and the Ge-covered region, mode mismatch occurs, resulting
in back-reflection. To address this issue, Global Foundries proposed an innovative
solution at the 2025 OFC Conference by optimizing the geometry of the Ge region to
redirect the reflected light away from the incident Si waveguide, thereby reducing
optical return losses (ORL) [1].
2. Reflection from the DBR: The inclusion of a DBR at the end of the APD reflects
the portion of light that is not fully absorbed during the first pass, allowing for
secondary absorption. However, since Ge cannot absorb all the incident light
completely, a small portion is inevitably reflected, resulting in optical reflections. A
case study on the Ansys official website also explains this phenomenon [2], attributing
it to diffraction in the Si waveguide and coupling between multiple optical modes,
which together contribute to the observed back-reflection.
The two mechanisms discussed above represent the primary sources of optical
interference in the detector. The resulting standing waves are mainly confined to the
detector structure and the incident silicon waveguide.
1. The photodetector operates as an intensity detector, primarily responding to
optical power through variations in photocurrent. Therefore, as long as the incident light
is absorbed by the Ge layer, effective detection can be achieved.
2. At the Si waveguide input, this phenomenon is known as ORL. Excessive ORL
can compromise the stability of the transmitter-side laser, potentially causing shifts in
the central wavelength and fluctuations in output power, thereby increasing the bit error
rate (BER) of the system [4]. To mitigate these effects, the IEEE 802.3 standard imposes
strict ORL requirements, specifying a maximum receiver-side reflectance of -12 dB [5].
3D-FDTD simulations of the APD structure revealed that the reflected optical
power is less than 0.56%, corresponding to an ORL of -22.5 dB. This value is well
below the threshold specified by the relevant standards, indicating that the device meets
the requirements for use in optical communication systems.
During testing, an 8° angled fiber-to-GC coupling configuration was employed to
effectively prevent reflected light in the Si waveguide from coupling back into the
optical fiber probe through the GC, thereby protecting the laser source from potential
damage. In practice, the device exhibited sufficiently low ORL, with no observable
adverse effects. Both small- and large-signal measurements were successful performed.
Additionally, a review of related studies on PDs revealed that optical back
reflections were present in many simulation results, though this phenomenon has
received limited attention. In future work, minimizing the ORL of the device will be a
key design objective.

Thank you for pointing out the ambiguous description here. We sincerely
apologize for this oversight in our writing. We intended to explain that we inserted a

varying width helps reduce additional loss caused by abrupt width transitions and the

a width of at least over 500 nm. This significant width mismatch between the two
waveguides makes a direct connection via a straight waveguide impractical, as it would
cause severe mode mismatch and refractive index discontinuity, resulting in increased
coupling loss.

8. Could the author explain the strategy for reducing the dark current? Also please
give an analysis about the noise.
Response:
In APDs, the dark current primarily consists of surface leakage current and bulk
dark current. The bulk dark current, which passes through the high electric field in the
multiplication region, is also multiplied. Therefore, to reduce the dark current of an
APD, we need to simultaneously reduce both surface leakage current and bulk dark
current. The main causes of surface leakage current are: 1. Surface defects, such as
dangling bonds; 2. High electric fields at the device surface, leading to increased
leakage current. However, compared to bulk dark current, surface leakage current is
relatively small because the bulk dark current is multiplied. Thus, to reduce the device's
dark current, the focus should be on reducing the bulk dark current. By reducing the
detector's volume and the ionization coefficient within the detector, the bulk dark
current can be effectively lowered. Therefore, in the manuscript, we have chosen Ge
with the smallest possible volume. Additionally, since Ge has a relatively high impact
ionization coefficient ratio k, we have employed a SACM structure, utilizing Ge for
detection and leveraging Si's low impact ionization coefficient ratio for avalanche
multiplication in Si. We have properly designed the doping location and concentration
to keep the electric field in Ge below the ionization threshold, successfully creating an
APD with low dark current.
Regarding noise, the primary sources of noise in APDs are excess noise and
multiplication gain, which lead to shot noise. The excess noise factor F is a function of
gain, F(M)=k M+(1−k) (2−1/M), where k is the impact ionization coefficient ratio and
M is the multiplication gain [1,2]. The ratio k is determined by k=β/α, where α and β
⋅ ⋅
are the electron and hole ionization coefficients of the semiconductor material in the
multiplication region [3]. Since Si has a lower k value, we have adopted the SACM
structure, which is advantageous for reducing excess noise.

Our design focuses on the TE mode primarily for its application in wavelength-
division multiplexing (WDM) receivers. Currently, WDM devices fabricated on Si
photonics platforms are polarization-sensitive due to the high birefringence of Si
waveguides. Therefore, before the light passes through the WDM demultiplexer, the

predominantly used on Si photonics platforms because Si waveguides have a stronger
confinement capability for this mode.

in Figure 11 [1], involves coupling both TE and TM polarized light into the photonic
chip simultaneously. A polarization splitter-rotator (PSR) is then used to separate the
TE and TM modes and rotate the TM mode to TE mode. The light is subsequently
demultiplexed and directed to the detector for further detection. The second scheme, as
shown in Figure 12 [2], employs a 2D polarization splitting grating coupler to
efficiently couple light of arbitrary polarization state and convert it entirely into the TE
polarization mode for transmission through the waveguide. After demultiplexing, the
light is detected by the PD.
After these processes, the polarization mode of the light detected by the PD is TE.
Therefore, our design primarily considers the optimal performance under the TE mode.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: As stated in my prior review, the primary claim in this paper is a Ge on Si avalanche photodiode with very high gain-bandwidth product. This requires an accurate determination of the gain, which in turn necessitates knowing the unity gain point accurately. I questioned the authors’ determination of the unity gain point and the response was, “The first method involves estimating the unit gain point by measuring the point where the second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to bias becomes zero [1, 2].” Reference 1 is a PhD dissertation titled, “Design, Characterization and Simulation of Avalanche Photodiodes” by Hektor Meier. There is no mention of this technique to find the unity gain point. The author does describe Monte Carlo simulations of avalanche photodiodes but there is no physical basis provided for the second derivative method. Reference 2 is the website for Lumerical software. The Lumerical model settings uses the second derivative method but there is no explanation for the basis of this approach. Lumerical is a great software tool but it is not trustworthy when applying a general rule to a broad range of materials. The authors also state that, “Currently, this method has been widely accepted and recognized by many prior works, including Nature Photonics [3, 4], Optica [5], Optical Fiber Communication Conference (OFC) [6], and European Conference on Optical Communication (ECOC) [7].” I am familiar with these references and they do not mention the second derivative method for determining the unity gain point. If the authors can provide a sound physical explanation for this gain determination technique, I cannot recommend publication because accurate determination of the gain is essential to their primary claim in this paper.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: 1. About the reply to comment #1 of the second reviewer. The authors have explained some minor difference between the present design and that in ref. 20 in the response letter. They have added some sentences to describe their structural design: “Figure 1(b) illustrates the cross-sectional doping profile of the Si-Ge APD, featuring a non-contact design between the Ge region and the Si-doped areas to effectively control the electric field within the Ge. Additionally, thicker metal interconnects are employed to further enhance device performance. The Ge absorption region dimensions are 9.1 μm (length) × 0.5 μm (width) × 0.26 μm (height).” However, the reviewer believes that this difference should be clearly described in the manuscript in order to make it clear to the readers. Furthermore, the authors should tell how the difference influences the device performances with some simulation and experimental verifications. For example, the authors only mention “non-contact design” once in the manuscript (page 2). They have never discussed how this design is related with their results. What is the optimal point for the non-contact design? Since this is the main difference, it is strongly suggested to have more details about it in the manuscript. 2. About EO responses at different optical powers. The experimental results in Fig. 3 only gave the measured OE responses of the APD at various reverse bias voltages under an input optical power of -16 dBm. However, the highest GBP was achieved at the optical power of -24 dBm. It is definitely necessary to show the measured EO responses at -24 dBm. More discussions should be given about the bandwidth reduction as the optical power decreases. 3. The GBP is the most important result considered in this paper. The authors should give more details in Fig. 3(d). For example, all data for different voltages should be given so that the readers can better understand the results. 4. The authors mentioned “To fully utilize this reflective effect, the Ge length was optimized to 9.1 μm, rather than 9.0 μm or 9.2 μm, as this specific length allows more unabsorbed light to be reflected and reabsorbed during a second pass.” Please show the simulation result on how the light absorption depends on the length. It means that the fabrication should be very accurate. How about the fabrication precision? Furthermore, if the light absorption is so sensitive to the length, would it also very sensitive to the cross-sectional dimensions (like the width, the thickness)? 5. About grating couplers. Grating couplers are playing an important role for evaluating the responsivity of the present APDs. The authors should give more results about the characterization of multiple GCs on the same chip, to show the uniformity in the wafer scale, so that it is reasonable to use the data from the reference devices. 6. About the responsivity. The authors mentioned “At a reverse bias of 3.5 V, the APD exhibits an optical internal responsivity of 0.75 A/W at unit gain, determined by comparison with a reference p-i-n PD fabricated on the same chip and sharing identical structural parameters, including Ge volume, waveguide dimensions, and GC design2,20,22,28”. In this design, the Ge thickness is chosen as 260 nm, which might be beneficial to enhance the device performance (e.g., bandwidth), as claimed by the authors (“The rationale behind choosing a smaller Ge volume is to reduce the transit time of photogenerated carriers in Ge, as well as to lower its capacitance). However, such a design lowers the light absorption in Ge. As the authors claimed, the Ge length should exceed 26.7 μm to achieve >90% light absorption. In this paper, the authors have chosen the length as 9.1 μm with the assistance of reflector. As a result, the responsivity is still relatively low (i.e., 0.75 A/W), much lower than the theoretical value of 1.06 A/W. Therefore, the authors should clarify that the GBP was achieved with a relatively low responsivity and also explain the reason in the revised manuscript (to response the second reviewer’s previous comment 6). Otherwise, if they extend the absorption length to achieve a higher responsivity, the bandwidth would be reduced and the GBP will also be reduced. 7. About the reflection (the second reviewer’s previous comment 3). The authors have given some explanation about the reflection. However, they should mention this in the revised manuscript to make everything clear, which is helpful for the readers. They should also tell how much the reflection is. 8. In addition, the authors mentioned that “an 8° angled fiber-to-GC coupling configuration was employed to effectively prevent reflected light in the Si waveguide from coupling back into the optical fiber probe through the GC, thereby protecting the laser source from potential damage.” One should realize that such 8° angled structures are not helpful to lower the reflected light from the rear grating. 9. About the previous comment “8. Could the author explain the strategy for reducing the dark current? Also please give an analysis about the noise.” The authors did not give the strategy for reducing the dark current in the revised manuscript. They should add it. Also, they just gave some general comments on the noise, while more results about the noise analysis should be given numerically or experimentally (experimental data are preferred). 10. About the previous comment “12. Please comment the polarization dependence of the present APD, which would be important for a receiver”. The authors have given a figure (Fig. 12) to show how polarization-insensitivity is achieved with the help of PSGCs. However, the present APD in this paper does not work bi-directionally because of the introduction of the rear reflectors.

We sincerely appreciate your insightful and constructive comments on our work.
Your observation is indeed well-founded, as the precise determination of the unity gain

In this work, the unity gain point was determined by comparing the performance

considered highly reliable, and its underlying rationale has been elaborated in our

Regarding the method of determining the unity gain point by identifying the
voltage at which the second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to the bias
voltage becomes zero, we would like to clarify that in our manuscript this approach is
primarily employed as an auxiliary means to further verify the correctness of the unity
gain point we selected.
The applicability of this method arises from the fact that, under optical
illumination, the current in an APD mainly consists of two components:
1. In the unity-gain stage, photogenerated carriers are driven by the electric field
to produce drift current without multiplication.
2. In the multiplication stage, once the device enters the avalanche region,
electrons or holes acquire sufficient energy to initiate impact ionization, thereby
triggering the avalanche process and resulting in current multiplication.
At low bias voltages, only carrier drift occurs, and the increase in current with bias
voltage is relatively slow, corresponding to a negative second derivative of photocurrent
with respect to bias voltage. As the voltage further increases and the electric field
becomes sufficiently strong, a fraction of the carriers reach the threshold energy for
impact ionization, causing a rapid acceleration in the current growth rate. At this critical
point, the second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to the bias voltage (i.e.,
the photocurrent generation acceleration) reaches zero, indicating that the APD has
entered the avalanche region.
To facilitate a more intuitive understanding of this method for the reviewer, we
have included the relevant content from the original referenced manuscripts in our
response (highlighted in bold) along with the corresponding citations.

1. Comparing the responsivity with that of a PIN PD.
Determining the unit gain point by comparing the responsivity of a PIN PD
fabricated on the same die and sharing identical structural parameters (such as the
length, width, and thickness of the Ge absorption region, as well as the length and width
of the Si waveguide). Currently, this method has been widely accepted and recognized
by many prior works, including Nature Photonics [1, 2], Optica [3], Optical Fiber
Communication Conference (OFC) [4], and European Conference on Optical
Communication (ECOC) [5].
This method is considered reliable because the responsivity of the PD is primarily
determined by the length of the Ge region and the coupling area. Although doping can
influence responsivity to some extent, the two devices in our comparison share exactly
the same heavily doped regions (in terms of concentration, area, and spacing). The only
difference lies in the lightly doped region, where n-type doping is replaced by p-type
doping. However, the influence of light doping on responsivity is minimal. Under such
conditions, the responsivity measured from the PIN device is nearly identical to the
initial responsivity of the APD.
2. Second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to the bias voltage becomes
zero.
Regarding the method of determining the unity gain point by identifying the
voltage at which the second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to the bias
voltage becomes zero [6,7], we would like to clarify that in our manuscript this
approach is primarily employed as an auxiliary means to further verify the correctness
of the unity gain point we selected.
The applicability of this method arises from the fact that, under optical
illumination, the current in an APD mainly consists of two components:
1. In the unity-gain stage, photogenerated carriers are driven by the electric field
to produce drift current without multiplication.
2. In the multiplication stage, once the device enters the avalanche region,
electrons or holes acquire sufficient energy to initiate impact ionization, thereby
triggering the avalanche process and resulting in current multiplication.
At low bias voltages, only carrier drift occurs, and the increase in current with bias
voltage is relatively slow, corresponding to a negative second derivative of photocurrent
with respect to bias voltage. As the voltage further increases and the electric field
becomes sufficiently strong, a fraction of the carriers reach the threshold energy for
impact ionization, causing a rapid acceleration in the current growth rate. At this critical
point, the second derivative of the photocurrent with respect to the bias voltage (i.e.,
the photocurrent generation acceleration) reaches zero, indicating that the APD has
entered the avalanche region.
Both methods can be used to determine the unity-gain point. In this work, we
determined the unity-gain point by comparing the responsivity of a PIN PD with that

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion, to which we have
also provided a simulation-based response. In a conventional PD (without a reflector at
the end), the absorption efficiency of Ge increases monotonically with length. However,
when a DBR is introduced at the end, the absorption efficiency of Ge no longer
increases simply with length; instead, it is influenced by both the coupling of the
evanescent wave and the position of the DBR. The key point is that when the Ge volume
is relatively small, the absorption efficiency is low, and secondary reflection is required
to enhance the responsivity. A higher responsivity is achieved only when a sufficient
amount of light is reflected. This effect is mainly determined by the length and thickness
of the Ge, and we will provide a detailed analysis of these factors separately.
First, we performed simulations to analyze the absorption of Ge with different
thicknesses, and the results are shown in Figure 2. It can be clearly observed that the
overall trend is that a thicker Ge layer leads to higher responsivity, while local
enhancements in absorption appear at certain specific thicknesses. Several
representative points were selected for detailed discussion. Figure 2(a) illustrates the
absorption for different Ge thicknesses under the same length condition. To more
intuitively present the optical field distribution at these points, seven typical positions
are marked in Figure 2(a). At points b, c, and d, the increase in absorption gradually
slows down. This is because, although increasing the Ge thickness enhances absorption,
the amount of light reflected back by the DBR decreases, thus reducing the growth rate
of responsivity. At point e, the absorption improvement induced by increasing Ge
thickness is insufficient to compensate for the reduced reflection from the DBR,
resulting in a lower absorption compared to point d. To further visualize the optical field
distribution, points f, g, and h were analyzed. At point g, more light is clearly reflected
by the DBR; while points f and h show nearly identical DBR reflections, the greater
thickness of the Ge layer at point h yields stronger intrinsic absorption, leading to higher
overall absorption than at point f.
Figure 2(a) shows the absorption for different Ge thicknesses under the same
length condition, while Figure 2(b)-(h) present the corresponding optical field
distributions at the selected points. The red arrows indicate the direction of input light,
and the DBR is located at the right end.

structure is shown in Figure 3. The red dashed line in Figure 3(a) represents the fitted
trend curve, which more intuitively illustrates the variation of responsivity with length.
Four representative points were selected for analysis, where b and d correspond to
relatively low absorption, while c and e correspond to relatively high absorption. By
examining the optical field distributions at points b, c, d, and e, it is evident that the
absorption of Ge is higher when the evanescent wave is fully coupled from Ge into Si.
Figure 3(a) shows the absorption for different Ge length under the same high
condition, while Figure 2(b)-(e) present the corresponding optical field distributions at
the selected points. The red arrows indicate the direction of input light, and the DBR is

With the incorporation of a rear DBR, the enhancement of the Ge absorption relies
on selecting an optimal combination of thickness and length. In the design, both the
height and length of the Ge layer were optimized to allow more light to enter the DBR
and be reflected back into the Ge, thereby maximizing absorption.
Regarding fabrication tolerance, the adopted platform is a 130-nm process.
Simulations show that near the maximum absorption point, length variations within

Table 1 provides an overview of state-of-the-art Ge APDs and Si-Ge APDs, which primarily operate
in the O-band and C-band wavelength ranges. Earlier studies proposed using the Ge region as the
multiplication region and integrating all PN junctions within the Ge of the APD5. However, this
approach suffered from excessive light absorption by dopants, resulting in insufficient responsivity.
To address this limitation, researchers developed a vertically structured Ge APD with simultaneous
Si-Ge doping, effectively reducing doping-induced absorption and enhancing responsivity24.
Despite these improvements, Ge APDs still face inherent challenges. When Ge is used as the
avalanche region, its high impact ionization coefficient ratio k leads to increased noise, dark current
and a limited GBP, thereby constraining the viability of Ge APDs as a mainstream solution5.
In contrast, Si-Ge APDs exhibit a lower effective impact ionization coefficient ratio k. A
reduced k is critical for minimizing the excess noise, thereby significantly improving the GBP and
sensitivity2,13. In SACM-structured Si-Ge APDs, the engineered electric field distribution confines
the multiplication region primarily to the Si layer, further reducing the effective k value and
effectively suppressing noise. Based on the electric field orientation, SACM Si-Ge APDs can be
classified into vertical and lateral configurations. The vertical SACM Si-Ge APD has undergone
substantial advancements through continuous optimization, achieving a relatively low avalanche
voltage, which is beneficial for APD applications6,13,14. However, its GBP remains modest, and its
fabrication process is more complex. Additionally, direct contact between Ge and the electrode can
degrade device performance. In contrast, the lateral SACM Si-Ge APD features a simpler fabrication

degradation7,20-23. Through ongoing research efforts, the GBP of lateral SACM Si-Ge APD has been

potential for practical applications.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: This manuscript describes a Si/Ge APD aiming to achieve a high GBP and to demonstrate high-symbol-rate eye diagrams. While the topic is important, several issues remain unclear, and the current version does not provide sufficient evidence to support the main claims. 1. This submission appears closely related to the authors’ OFC 2025 paper (M4K.5). If this is an extended version, it should be clearly stated, and the differences must be explained. 2.The main new element seems to be the 8-channel array, but key points are missing: whether the channels were operated simultaneously, the level of crosstalk, and any wavelength dependence across the O-band. These aspects should be clarified. 3. The TDECQ values in Fig. 5 appear low. It is also unclear why the eyes open despite the device bandwidth (30–35 GHz) being lower than the Nyquist rate for 100-GBaud PAM-4. The manuscript should state whether any equalization or signal processing was used. 4. The manuscript suggests that the non-contact design drastically improves performance, but the mechanism and effect are not clearly explained. If the excess-noise factor corresponds to k ≈ 0.05, the authors should discuss with such as simulations whether such a value reasonably leads to a GBP above 7000 GHz. 5. In Fig. 3, F is extracted at low M that do not match the operating point used for the GBP measurement. k should be evaluated at the relevant M to support the argument.

measurement chain are significantly amplified, which can compromise the accurate
extraction of the excess noise factor F and obscure the intrinsic avalanche noise
characteristics of the device. Therefore, characterizing the k value under low-gain
conditions is a commonly adopted and more reliable approach in APD noise analysis,
as evidenced by multiple prior studies that have employed the same experimental
strategy [8-11].

measured at a high multiplication gain (M) operating point and is not inferred from the

Section 1, "Introduction"
In this paper, we present a high-speed Si-Ge APD with a record-breaking GBP of 7564 GHz,
surpassing the highest previously reported value. Utilizing a lateral SACM structure, we designed
an APD that spatially separates the Ge absorption region from the doped regions. By minimizing
the electric field in Ge while maintaining efficient carrier transport and multiplication, we
significantly reduced dark current. To further enhance device responsivity, we incorporated a
tapered waveguide at the front end and a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) at the rear. Experimental
results show that under a reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V, the APD exhibits an ultra-low dark current
of 8.4 μA, and achieves a maximum GBP of 7564 GHz at an input optical power of -24 dBm, while
maintaining a low effective k value of 0.05. We evaluated the APD’s performance for high-speed
signals, achieving clear eye diagrams for 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps non-return-to-zero (NRZ) signals,
as well as 128 Gbps and 200 Gbps four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) signals. The APD
demonstrated excellent sensitivity, achieving -20.8 dBm and -17.1 dBm for 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps
NRZ signals, respectively, which meet the hard-decision forward error correction (HD-FEC)
threshold of BER = 3.8×10−3. For 128 Gbps and 200 Gbps PAM4 signals, the sensitivities were -
14.2 dBm and -9.6 dBm, respectively, also within the HD-FEC limit. Furthermore, we conducted
high-speed eye diagram validation for 200 Gbps PAM4 signals across eight APDs, each tuned to
the specific wavelengths required for eight-channel dense wavelength division multiplexing
(DWDM). This manuscript represents a substantial extension of our previous OFC work25,
expanding the study from a single-channel device to an eight-channel APD array, and providing
detailed design and analysis, along with a further systematic investigation of excess-noise
characteristics. These remarkable results highlight the immense potential of this APD for
applications in optical communications, quantum technology, LiDAR, and beyond.

## Introduction

Avalanche photodetectors are highly valued for their high bandwidth, high gain, and compact integration, making them
widely applicable in optical communications, optical interconnects, light detection and ranging (LiDAR) systems,
quantum computing, and biosensing1-3. As artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, and cloud computing continue
to expand rapidly, the demand for computational power and high-speed data transmission in large-scale data centers and
high-performance computing (HPC) is growing exponentially4-6. This surge has intensified the need for transceivers with
higher bandwidth density. However, current optical link and power budgets are struggling to keep pace with these
escalating demands4. As a pivotal component in optical receivers, APDs play a crucial role in enhancing link performance
by providing internal gain, which helps reduce power consumption and optimize signal integrity. These characteristics
are essential for advancing optical receiver systems toward higher bandwidth and lower power operation7,8.

Gain bandwidth product (GBP) is a key metric in evaluating APD performance in high-speed optical communication
and is strongly influenced by the impact ionization coefficient ratio. While most III-V materials exhibit an impact
ionization coefficient ratio in the range of k ≈ 0.1-19,10 , silicon (Si) stands out with an exceptionally low ratio of k ≈
0.0211,12. However, Si’s cutoff wavelength of 1100 nm limits efficient photo-carrier generation in fiber communication
wavelengths, necessitating alternative materials. Germanium (Ge) is a preferred material for silicon-based PDs due to its
superior absorption efficiency at fiber communication wavelengths and higher carrier mobility compared to Si. However,
the impact ionization coefficient ratio of Ge (k ≈ 1)13,14 is significantly higher, potentially leading to increased noise. To
leverage the high absorption of Ge while benefiting from the low ionization coefficient ratio of Si, researchers have
proposed APDs with separate absorption charge multiplication (SACM) structures15. Fabricated on a standard silicon-
on-insulator (SOI) platform, the Si-Ge APD offers higher gain, excellent sensitivity, and superior integration density,
making it an optimal choice for high-performance optical receivers16,17.

In current SACM structure research, vertical SACM-type APDs require metal electrode deposition on the Ge
surface18,19. However, this approach induces Fermi-level pinning, degrading the ohmic contact and increasing contact
resistance. Additionally, the metal presence on the Ge surface introduces more dangling bonds, leading to higher leakage
current, which in turn reduces device responsivity and increases noise. Moreover, metal contacts facilitate additional
photogenerated carrier recombination, further compromising optoelectronic performance. In contrast, lateral SACM Si-
Ge APDs mitigate these challenges while also simplifying fabrication. Dai et al. proposed a series of lateral SACM Si-
Ge APDs, demonstrating a significant GBP improvement from 615 GHz20 to 1440 GHz21, and later to 3036 GHz22. This
progression has provided valuable insights into GBP enhancement strategies. However, this design still exhibits relatively
high dark current at the operating voltage, which can hinder the achievement of higher sensitivity and gain. A recent
study reported an improved lateral SACM Si-Ge APD with a bandwidth of 53 GHz and a GBP of 1033 GHz23. The high
bandwidth was achieved by incorporating a large inductor (~700 pH) into the APD electrode through inductive peaking.
However, in the SACM structure, the multiplication gain and GBP remain constrained by the Ge-Si doping contact due
to the high dark current resulting from significant tunneling currents at high voltages. Additionally, this approach may
introduce challenges in impedance matching with the transimpedance amplifier S(TIA) and signal transmission. Currently,
researchers continue exploring various strategies to further enhance APSD GBP for higher-speed and higher-gain
detection24. However, achieving a significantly higher GBP remains a crEitical and challenging research direction.

In this work, we present a high-speed Si-Ge APD with a reRcord-breaking GBP of 7564 GHz, which exceeds
previously reported values. Utilizing a lateral SACM structurPe, we design an APD that spatially separates the Ge
absorption region from the doped regions. By minimizing th e electric field in Ge while maintaining efficient carrier
transport and multiplication, the dark current is significantly reduced. To further enhance device responsivity, we
incorporate a tapered waveguide at the front end and a distributed Bragg reflector (DBR) at the rear. Experimental results
show that under a reverse bias voltage of 12.5 V, Ethe APD exhibits a dark current of 8.4 μA and achieves a maximum
GBP of 7564 GHz at an input optical power of L-24 dBm, while maintaining a low effective k value of 0.05. We evaluate
the APD performance for high-speed signals and obtain clear eye diagrams for 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps non-return-to-
zero (NRZ) signals, as well as 128 Gbps and 200 Gbps four-level pulse amplitude modulation (PAM4) signals. The APD
also exhibits high sensitivity, achieving -20.8 dBm and -17.1 dBm for 64 Gbps and 100 Gbps NRZ signals, respectively,
both of which meet the hard-decision forward error correction (HD-FEC) threshold of BER = 3.8×10−3. For 128 Gbps
and 200 Gbps PAM4 signals, the sensitivities are -14.2 dBm and -9.6 dBm, respectively, both within the HD-FEC limit.
Furthermore, we perform high-speed eye diagram measurements for 200 Gbps PAM4 signals across eight APDs, each
tuned to the specific wavelengths required for eight-channel dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM). This
manuscript represents a substantial extension of our previous OFC work25, expanding the study from a single-channel
device to an eight-channel APD array, and providing detailed design and analysis, along with a further systematic
investigation of excess-noise characteristics. These remarkable results highlight the immense potential of this APD for
applications in optical communications, quantum technology, LiDAR, and beyond.

---

## Results

Device Structure and Design
Figure 1(a) presents a three-dimensional (3D) schematic of the lateral p+-i-p-n+ doped SACM Si-Ge APD, incorporating
a DBR at the rear to enhance device responsivity. The design process begins with optimizing the electric field distribution
to achieve high performance. Figure 1(b) illustrates the cross-sectional doping profile of the Si-Ge APD, featuring a non-
contact design between the Ge region and the Si-doped areas to effectively control the electric field within the Ge. To
quantitatively describe this non-contact design strategy, we optimize the doping positions on the rib waveguide, denoted
as Wp and ΔW, respectively. Additionally, thicker metal interconnects are employed to further enhance device
performance. The Ge absorption region dimensions are 9.1 μm (length) × 0.5 μm (width) × 0.26 μm (height). Given Ge's
high impact ionization coefficient, optimization efforts focus on the doping regions adjacent to the Ge layer, specifically
adjusting the widths of Wp and ΔW. The primary goal is to maximize ionization within Si while suppressing ionization
in Ge, requiring the electric field strength in Si to exceed 3×10⁷ V/m, while ensuring it remains below 2×10⁷ V/m in
Ge26,27. Additionally, to facilitate efficient carrier transport at saturation velocity within Ge, the electric field in Ge is
designed to exceed 1×10⁶ V/m 28.

The electric field design begins with optimizing the multiplication region doping width Wp to maintain a high
electric field within the multiplication region while preventing its extension into the absorption region. Figure 1(c) depicts
the electric field distribution along the black cutline of the ridge waveguide in Figure 1(b) under varying Wp conditions.
As the Wp increases, the electric field strength in the multiplication region rises, but the high electric field region
gradually shifts toward the absorption region, potentially increasing the electric field in Ge and degrading device
performance. To balance these effects, Wp is set at 225 nm. Next, ΔW is optimized to confine the electric field effectively
within the charge region. Figure 1(d) illustrates the electric field distribution along the black cutline of the ridge
waveguide in Figure 1(b) under different p+ doping width conditions, with anS inset providing a magnified view of the
localized region. If the doping position is too far from the Ge layer, the eSlectric field is not fully confined within the
charge region, potentially inducing additional current in the Si-doped arEea and increasing the device's shot noise. Based
on the above considerations, i.e., to ensure effective confinement ofR the optical field, ΔW is set to 110 nm.

To further enhance performance, graded doping is emploPyed to reduce resistance and capacitance. The p-type
doping concentrations are set at 7.1 × 1019 cm-3 (p++), 5.3 × 1018 cm-3 (p+), and 2.1 × 1017 cm-3 (p), while the n-type
doping concentrations are set at 1.0 × 1020 cm-3 (n++) and 1.0 × 1019 cm-3 (n+), respectively. Additionally, a lateral
structure is adopted to minimize light absorption by metal electrodes and reduce dark current caused by defects near the
heterojunction under breakdown voltage conditioEns. The inset in Figure 1(b) presents the simulated cross-sectional
electric field results under a reverse bias of 12.L5 V, confirming effective electric field confinement. Through optimized
doping position and concentration, together with precise control of Wp and ΔW enabled by the non-contact design, the
high electric field is effectively confined within the Si multiplication region, while the Ge absorption region is maintained
at a relatively low electric field, thereby achieving precise electric-field engineering. Under this field configuration,
avalanche multiplication is dominated by an electron-driven quasi-unipolar mechanism, in which impact ionization in Si
is maximized whereas ionization in Ge is strongly suppressed. As a result, the excess noise is effectively reduced and the
overall device performance is significantly enhanced.

The APD couples O-band optical signals from the Si waveguide into Ge. To mitigate coupling loss caused by abrupt
width changes between the Si and Ge waveguides, a tapered waveguide is employed. Traditionally, increasing Ge volume
has been a primary method for enhancing responsivity. However, as the volume of Ge increases, the carrier transit time
is prolonged, reducing the response speed and adversely impacting the device's electrical performance. To address this
issue, we integrate a DBR at the rear and incorporated a tapered waveguide at the front to confine more light within the
absorption region, thereby enabling secondary light absorption and improving overall responsivity.

The DBR structure in this device is a first-order DBR, chosen for its low scattering losses and high reflectivity. As
depicted in Figure 1(e), when the number of grating periods reaches five, the reflectivity exceeds 90%, effectively
reflecting light at the tail. The inset in Figure 1(e) illustrates that, with five grating periods, the operational wavelength
range extends from 1100 nm to 1700 nm, perfectly covering the O-band. Figure 2 presents 3D finite-difference time-
domain (FDTD) simulation results for two APD structures. The evanescently coupled optical field distributions for APDs
without and with a DBR are shown in Figures 2(a) and (c), respectively. In the absence of a DBR, significant light leakage
occurs at the end of the APD. In contrast, incorporating a DBR significantly reduces this leakage by reflecting the
unabsorbed light back into the Ge region, thereby enhancing responsivity. To fully utilize this reflective effect, the Ge
length is optimized to 9.1 μm (see Supplementary Note 1), rather than 9.0 μm or 9.2 μm, as this specific length allows
more unabsorbed light to be reflected and reabsorbed during a second pass. However, standing waves are observed in
the field distribution, mainly due to mode mismatch between the Si waveguide and Ge layer as well as reflections from
the rear DBR. Simulations indicate that the optical return loss (ORL) of this device is -22.5 dB (see Supplementary Note
2). To further verify the effect of the DBR, top-view field distributions in Figures 2(b) and 2(d) show that the inclusion
of the DBR significantly increases the optical intensity in the Ge absorption region. The inclusion of a five-period DBR
at the rear enhances the overall light confinement within the Ge layer. Additionally, a front-end tapered waveguide is
employed to minimize input reflection losses. As a result, the device's responsivity improves by 35%.

Static Measurements
Figure 3(a) shows the I-V characteristics of the fabricated Si-Ge APD under various bias voltages, both with and without
incident light, with optical power ranging from -26 dBm to -12 dBm. The grating couplers (GCs) used in this work are
characterized using a test structure consisting of a pair of GCs connected by a short straight waveguide. The measured
insertion loss is 6.0 dB/facet at 1310 nm. At a reverse bias of 3.5 V, the APD exShibits an optical internal responsivity of
0.75 A/W at unit gain, determined by comparison with a reference p-i-n PSD fabricated on the same chip and sharing
